facts.raw_span: A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia
he had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering”
two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015
biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
he reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges
abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV
after angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved
follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma
MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis
A 64-year-old white man was admitted in March 2016 with acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia
he had been on therapeutic anticoagulation for paroxysmal “pre-shimmering”
two hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, first noted in August 2015
biopsies at that time showed histologically proven adenoma without malignancy
he was hemodynamically stable but had a hemoglobin level of 4.4 mmol/L
he reported no weight loss, fever, or constitutional symptoms
α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels within normal ranges
abdominal ultrasound revealed subcapsular hepatic bleeding
contrast-enhanced CT confirmed active bleeding from one of the two hypervascular lesions in segment IV
after angiographic embolization and conservative management, bleeding resolved
follow-up CT showed persistent hypervascular lesions without typical features of hepatocellular carcinoma
MRI demonstrated hypervascular lesions with central necrosis

concepts.why: The patient has a history of hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, which were biopsied and shown to be adenomas without malignancy, and now presents with active bleeding from one of these lesions.
The patient presents with anemia, which is likely related to the chronic disease process, given the lack of other obvious causes such as bleeding or nutritional deficiencies.
The patient presents with acute-onset abdominal pain, which is likely related to the active bleeding from the hepatic adenoma.
The patient has a history of hypervascular liver lesions in segment IV, which are persistent on follow-up imaging, and may represent a hypervascular liver lesion such as a hemangioma.

rationales.F01: Acute-onset abdominal pain and anemia suggest a possible hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage or acute abdominal pain.
rationales.F03: Hypervascular liver lesions are characteristic of hepatic adenoma and hypervascular liver lesions.
rationales.F04: Histologically proven adenoma without malignancy supports the diagnosis of hepatic adenoma.
rationales.F07: Normal tumor markers make hepatocellular carcinoma less likely, but do not rule out hepatic adenoma.
rationales.F08: Subcapsular hepatic bleeding is consistent with hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage.
rationales.F09: Active bleeding from a hypervascular lesion confirms the diagnosis of hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's history of hypervascular liver lesions, histologically proven adenoma, and evidence of active bleeding from one of these lesions, as confirmed by imaging studies, strongly supports this diagnosis.
